One of the most striking images from the U.S.’s high-wire diplomatic talks in recent days was a photograph of Jared Kushner in Moscow posted by a Russian negotiator .

   Standing on the Russian tarmac in front of a U.S. government plane, there was Kushner, with tousled hair, dark slacks, and white Nikes. He was shaking hands with Russia’s Kirill Dmitriev. Like Kushner, Dmitriev straddles a world between politics and government and is seen as vital to any effort to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

   Kushner is one of President Trump’s sons-in-law and is famously very close to the commander in chief. He didn’t have much geopolitical experience until his father-in-law became president in 2017 but then became involved in all sorts of negotiations, from trade wars to real wars.

   As soon as Trump left office in 2021, Kushner launched an investment fund, Affinity Partners, where he continues to serve as chief executive. According to Trump’s Board of Peace, on which Kushner serves as an “ executive board member ,” Affinity has more than $5 billion in assets under management. And his initial investors included a heavy dose of Middle Eastern money.

   This has led Democrats to allege there’s a “ conflict of interest ,” but Kushner hasn’t been slowed. He appears more influential than ever. (In fact, he recently met with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, showing that his diplomatic skills can be put to use for challenges both foreign and domestic.)

   In public, Kushner comes across as a “good cop,” with bright smiles and careful nods. He explained his approach this weekend while taking questions alongside presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukraine’s leader Volodymyr Zelensky. (Kushner spent time in both Russia and Ukraine in recent days.) Kushner doesn’t wag fingers in people’s faces (in public, at least).

   “You know President Trump comes from the business world,” Kushner said this weekend. “In the business world, you think about things in the context of win-win. You know, how do you create opportunities for both sides to do what’s in their interests? War is a negative sum, you know everyone loses from war, whereas you know business and peace is positive sum. You can find big benefits from that in a big way.”

   CIA Director John Ratcliffe recently visited Moscow, a move that some viewed as recognition that the Kushner-Witkoff outreach had sputtered. Kushner and Witkoff have been trying to find off-ramps for this war for some time, with little to show for it.

   This weekend, Kushner and Witkoff left their talks in Ukraine on a train that was called the “Peace Express” on the display board. Both had big smiles on their faces.

   Rep. Mike Collins : Scandals are weighing on the Georgia Republican’s bid to topple Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in the Senate race.

A wide-ranging probe by the Department of Homeland Security’s internal watchdog is scrutinizing any potential improprieties in the contracting process.    A Trump-aligned group is pouring money into Texas. The president’s super PAC has entered the competitive Senate race in the state with a $10 million ad buy to back Republican Ken Paxton and oppose his Democratic challenger, James Talarico. The aid from MAGA Inc. is a start, but far short of the money Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is expected to need in an expensive campaign state.

The organization has experienced explosive growth in recent years, particularly since the election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

   • The Supreme Court agreed to hear cases filed by two men who petitioned the court without legal representation.

Jared Kushner Is Now One of World’s Most Powerful Diplomats
 
Plus, Trump calls for New Mexico’s name change, and Corey Lewandowski’s power moves at DHS
 
 
VALENTYN OGIRENKO/REUTERS
 

Good morning. One of the most striking images from the U.S.’s high-wire diplomatic talks in recent days was a photograph of Jared Kushner in Moscow posted by a Russian negotiator.

 

Standing on the Russian tarmac in front of a U.S. government plane, there was Kushner, with tousled hair, dark slacks, and white Nikes. He was shaking hands with Russia’s Kirill Dmitriev. Like Kushner, Dmitriev straddles a world between politics and government and is seen as vital to any effort to end the Russia-Ukraine war.

 

Kushner is one of President Trump’s sons-in-law and is famously very close to the commander in chief. He didn’t have much geopolitical experience until his father-in-law became president in 2017 but then became involved in all sorts of negotiations, from trade wars to real wars.

 

As soon as Trump left office in 2021, Kushner launched an investment fund, Affinity Partners, where he continues to serve as chief executive. According to Trump’s Board of Peace, on which Kushner serves as an “executive board member,” Affinity has more than $5 billion in assets under management. And his initial investors included a heavy dose of Middle Eastern money.

 

This has led Democrats to allege there’s a “conflict of interest,” but Kushner hasn’t been slowed. He appears more influential than ever. (In fact, he recently met with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, showing that his diplomatic skills can be put to use for challenges both foreign and domestic.)

 

In public, Kushner comes across as a “good cop,” with bright smiles and careful nods. He explained his approach this weekend while taking questions alongside presidential envoy Steve Witkoff and Ukraine’s leader Volodymyr Zelensky. (Kushner spent time in both Russia and Ukraine in recent days.) Kushner doesn’t wag fingers in people’s faces (in public, at least).

 

“You know President Trump comes from the business world,” Kushner said this weekend. “In the business world, you think about things in the context of win-win. You know, how do you create opportunities for both sides to do what’s in their interests? War is a negative sum, you know everyone loses from war, whereas you know business and peace is positive sum. You can find big benefits from that in a big way.”

 

CIA Director John Ratcliffe recently visited Moscow, a move that some viewed as recognition that the Kushner-Witkoff outreach had sputtered. Kushner and Witkoff have been trying to find off-ramps for this war for some time, with little to show for it.

 

This weekend, Kushner and Witkoff left their talks in Ukraine on a train that was called the “Peace Express” on the display board. Both had big smiles on their faces.

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

New Mexico: Trump is calling for changing the state’s name to New America, though he doesn’t have the power to force the switch.

 

Rep. Mike Collins: Scandals are weighing on the Georgia Republican’s bid to topple Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in the Senate race.

 

Trump’s Tuesday: The president is scheduled to participate in a Steel Across America event at 10:35 a.m. ET. He will spend his afternoon taking part in policy meetings.

What I’m Following

 
 
VALERIE PLESCH/BLOOMBERG NEWS
 

Corey Lewandowski allegedly pitched government services to Qatar and the U.A.E. for personal gain as a top DHS adviser. A wide-ranging probe by the Department of Homeland Security’s internal watchdog is scrutinizing any potential improprieties in the contracting process. Lewandowski’s representative denied that he sought contracts with foreign governments or played any role in DHS contract reviews.

 

A Trump-aligned group is pouring money into Texas. The president’s super PAC has entered the competitive Senate race in the state with a $10 million ad buy to back Republican Ken Paxton and oppose his Democratic challenger, James Talarico. The aid from MAGA Inc. is a start, but far short of the money Paxton, the state’s attorney general, is expected to need in an expensive campaign state.

 

The DSA is leaning on social events to convert the curious. “Coffee With Comrades” and “socialist softball” are examples of an endless buffet of social events the Democratic Socialists of America uses to attract new members and more closely bind existing ones to the movement. The organization has experienced explosive growth in recent years, particularly since the election of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Many MAGA-centered merchandise retailers and suppliers are experiencing a significant decline in sales during Trump’s second term.

 

• The Supreme Court agreed to hear cases filed by two men who petitioned the court without legal representation.

 

• Vice President JD Vance called AI satanic—he struck a chord among Christian Republicans.
